# Introduction

# How To
## Core Differences Between R and Python Syntax

## Worked Example
To practice the different syntax, we will work through an example using a data set of 2023 college football data. The data can be found in the GitHub repository data folder or on Kaggle at this [link](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/jeffgallini/college-football-team-stats-2019?resource=download&select=cfb23.csv). Below we simply are loading the data in. We start by importing the pandas package which is equivalent to loading in a library such as `tidyverse` in R. We then load the data set in using `pd.read_csv`.
```{python}
# import pandas (equivalent to loading in libraries in R)
import pandas as pd
# import matplotlib for plotting (like ggplot but isn't included in pandas)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plot

# loading in data
data = pd.read_csv("data/cfb23.csv")

# check the head and tail of the data to make sure it loaded in correctly
data.head(6)
```

```{python}
data.tail(6)
```

After loading in the data, we want to check to make sure it was loaded in properly. We do this using `head` and `tail`. The syntax is just slightly different in Python as you can see above, however it is relatively similar. 
```{python}
# shape of the data frame
data.shape
```

`.shape` returns a tuple with dimensions of the pandas data frame. It is an attribute, not a function and that is why we don't use `()`. 
```{python}
# count number of na's for each variable
data.isna().sum()
```



## Common Syntax Errors

## Cheat Sheet Guide
| Operation | R (`dplyr`/ Base R) | Python (`pandas`) | Helpful Notes |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| Inspect types | `glimpse(df)` / `str(df)`| `df.info()` or `df.dtypes` | `.dtypes` has no parentheses |
| Select columns | `select(df, a, b)` | `df[['a', 'b']]` | Requires double brackets `[[]]` |
| Filter Rows | `filter(df, a > 5 & b < 10)` | `df[(df['a'] > 5) & (df['b'] < 10)]` | Must use `&` and warp conditions in `()` |
| Range filter | `filter(between(a, 5, 10))` | `df[df['a'].between(5, 10)]` | Inclusive on both ends by default |
| Distinct count | `n_distinct(df$col)` | `df['col'].nunique()` | Don't use `.count()` |
| Frequency table | `count(df, col)` | `df['col'].value_counts()` | Returns counts per unique value |
